## Meet the data:

::: {.callout-tip title="Cafe Orders"}
A campus cafe owner has given us two weeks of orders (November 1 to 14). He wants to know how the business has been performing, but the data is messy.
:::


Each row is *one customer*. Each column is *one variable*.


## Data description (i){.smaller}

The `sales` table:

| Variable | Type | Description |
|---|---|---------|
| `customer_id` | ID | Customer number |
| `date` | Date | Day of the order (November 1 to 14, 2026) |
| `time` | Time | Time of the order. The cafe is open from 8:00 to 6:00 |
| `item` | Categorical | Drink ordered (6 drinks) |
| `revenue` | Numeric (dollars) | What the customer paid, including any tip |
| `payment` | Categorical | How they paid |
| `rating` | Ordinal (1-5) | Rating from 1 (worst) to 5 (best) |


## Data description (ii){.smaller}

The `drinks` table has **one row per drink**. It lets you look up facts about each drink.

| Variable | Type | Description |
|---|---|------|
| `item` | Categorical | Drink name (same as in `sales`) |
| `price` | Numeric (dollars) | Menu price of one drink |
| `caffeine_mg` | Numeric | Caffeine in the drink (mg) |
| `has_dairy` | Binary | Does it contain dairy? (Yes / No) |
| `prop_sales` | Numeric | Share of the cafe's sales this drink had historically |


## The five questions

1. Do weekend days have more customers per day than weekdays?
2. What is the most popular drink in the morning and in the afternoon?
3. Which payment method has the highest average tip, and which has the most customers who gave a rating?
4. Do actual drink sales match the cafe's historical proportions?
5. **Fun Challenge:** A "lucky" customer gets a gift mug if their order is placed at exactly ":13" past the hour. Which drink do lucky customers choose most often, and what is their average rating compared with everyone else's?


# Why we cannot just answer the questions

## The raw data

```{webr}
glimpse(sales)
```

- Nothing crashed. But can we trust this data?


## Try the questions on the raw data

```{webr}
# Q1: how many different dates? (The cafe was open for 14 days.)
# sales |> count(date) |> nrow()

# Q3: how many payment methods? (The cafe takes 3.)
# sales |> count(payment)

# Q3: the average revenue?
# mean(sales$revenue)

# Q5: the average rating? (Ratings go from 1 to 5.)
# mean(sales$rating)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="No error, but the wrong answer"}
Most of these code *ran*. They just gave us nonsense. That is why the data needs fixing before we do anything meaningful with it.
:::

# The toolbox

## How the toolbox works

::: {.callout-note title="These are small examples, not exactly your data"}
Each slide has a tiny messy example, what goes wrong with it, and the function that fixes it. The examples are about bakeries and libraries, **not** cafes.

Click **Run Code**, then change the numbers and words to see what happens.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Your job"}
Spot the similar problems in the cafe data, and potentially apply the same tool.
:::


## Text that should be numbers

::: {.callout-note title="`parse_number()`"}
Turns text with extra symbols into a number.
:::

```{webr}
x <- c("$1523.05", "243", "34,234")

mean(x)                # text has no average
parse_number(x)
mean(parse_number(x))
```


## Same thing, but different spelling

::: {.callout-note title="`str_to_lower()`"}
Makes all the letters lower case, so one thing has one spelling.
:::

```{webr}
pets <- tibble(pet = c("Dog", "dog", "Cat", "cat", "DOG"))

pets |> count(pet)                                  # 5 spellings, 2 pets

pets |>
  mutate(pet = str_to_lower(pet)) |>
  count(pet)
```


## A number that means "missing"

::: {.callout-note title="`na_if(x, value)`"}
Turns one special value into `NA`. Then `na.rm = TRUE` ignores it.
:::

```{webr}
pages <- c(12, 30, -1, 25, -1)     # -1 means "did not answer"

mean(pages)                         # too low!
pages_clean <- na_if(pages, -1)
pages_clean
mean(pages_clean, na.rm = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How do I find the special number?"}
Look at `summary()` of the column. A 1-to-5 rating should not have a minimum far below 1.
:::


## Some date formats

::: {.callout-note title="`ymd()`, `dmy()`, `str_sub()`"}
`ymd()` reads year-first dates and `dmy()` reads day-first dates. `str_sub(x, 1, 4)` takes the first 4 characters.
:::

```{webr}
d <- c("2026-03-14", "14-03-2026", "2026-05-02", "02-05-2026")

ymd(d)                                    # the day-first ones fail
str_sub(d, 1, 4)                          # year-first starts with 2026

if_else(str_sub(d, 1, 4) == "2026", ymd(d), dmy(d))
```

- `if_else(condition, value if TRUE, value if FALSE)`
- You may see a "failed to parse" warning. That's okay.


## Which day of the week?

::: {.callout-note title="`wday()`"}
Gets the day of the week from a date. With `week_start = 1`, Monday is 1 and Sunday is 7.
:::

```{webr}
days <- ymd(c("2026-03-12", "2026-03-14", "2026-03-15"))

wday(days, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE)     # the names
wday(days, week_start = 1)                  # the numbers

# How do I figure out if my data set contains the days I need?

```


## Time without AM or PM

::: {.callout-note title="`separate_wider_delim()`"}
Splits one column into two at a symbol, like `:`. Then `as.numeric()` turns the pieces into numbers.
:::

m
```{webr}
library_times <- tibble(time = c("9:15", "11:40", "12:05", "3:20", "4:45"))

library_times |>
  separate_wider_delim(time, delim = ":", names = c("hh", "mm")) |>
  mutate(
    hh = as.numeric(hh),
    mm = as.numeric(mm),
    hour24 = NA,
    period = NA
  )
```




## The top item in each group

::: {.callout-note title="`group_by()` and `slice_max()`"}
`slice_max(n, n = 1)` keeps the row with the biggest `n` in each group.
:::

```{webr}
bakery <- tibble(
  period = c("am", "am", "am", "pm", "pm", "pm", "pm"),
  item   = c("Bagel", "Bagel", "Scone", "Scone", "Scone", "Bagel", "Muffin")
)

bakery |> count(period, item)

bakery |>
  count(period, item) |>
  group_by(period) |>
  slice_max(n, n = 1)
```
